body:
Why Objects Feel Lighter in Water

A stone feels easier to support when it is immersed in water than when it is held in air. A tightly closed empty plastic bottle pushed beneath the water surface tends to rise when released.

Both observations occur because water exerts an upward force on immersed objects. This force acts against the object's weight.

Buoyancy is the phenomenon in which a fluid exerts an upward force on an object immersed in it. This force is called buoyant force or upthrust.

Buoyancy occurs in liquids and gases. Therefore, an object immersed in water experiences buoyancy, and objects surrounded by air also experience a smaller buoyant force.

Why Buoyant Force Acts Upward

Pressure in a stationary liquid increases with depth. Consequently, the lower surface of a submerged object generally experiences greater liquid pressure than its upper surface.

The upward forces produced on the lower surface therefore exceed the downward forces produced on the upper surface. The resulting net force from the surrounding fluid is upward.

The direction of buoyant force is consequently vertically upward, opposite to the direction of gravitational acceleration.

What Determines the Magnitude of Buoyant Force?

The buoyant force depends on the amount of fluid displaced, the fluid's density and the local gravitational acceleration.

As a floating object is pushed farther into water, the volume of water displaced increases until the object becomes fully submerged. The buoyant force increases as the displaced volume increases.

Once a rigid object is completely submerged, its displaced volume remains the same. In a liquid of approximately uniform density, the buoyant force therefore remains approximately unchanged when the object is moved deeper.

For a fully submerged rigid object in the same liquid, increasing depth does not automatically increase buoyant force. The greater fluid pressure at depth acts on both the upper and lower surfaces; the buoyant force depends on their resulting difference.

Archimedes' Principle

Archimedes was an ancient Greek mathematician and scientist whose name is associated with the principle of buoyancy.

Archimedes' principle: A body immersed fully or partially in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by that body.

The principle may be expressed as:

$$F_{\mathrm{b}}=\rho_{\mathrm{fluid}}V_{\mathrm{displaced}}g$$

Here, \(F_{\mathrm{b}}\) is the buoyant force, \(\rho_{\mathrm{fluid}}\) is the density of the fluid, \(V_{\mathrm{displaced}}\) is the displaced fluid volume and \(g\) is the local gravitational acceleration.

This equation follows from the principle that buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid. The displaced fluid's mass is its density multiplied by its volume, and its weight is that mass multiplied by g.

Displacement and Buoyancy

Consider a rigid block with a volume of 0.002 m3 completely immersed in water. Its volume of displaced water is also 0.002 m3.

Taking water's density as approximately 1000 kg/m3, the mass of displaced water is:

$$m=1000\times0.002=2\;\mathrm{kg}$$

The weight of this displaced water is:

$$W=2\times9.8=19.6\;\mathrm{N}$$

Therefore, the buoyant force on the fully immersed block is approximately 19.6 N.

This result depends on the displaced water, not directly on whether the block itself is made of wood, plastic or metal.

Apparent Weight in a Fluid

When an object is supported while immersed in water, its downward weight is partly opposed by upward buoyant force. Therefore, the supporting force needed to hold it is smaller than it would be without buoyancy.

For a stationary object supported by a vertical spring balance:

$$W_{\mathrm{apparent}}=W_{\mathrm{actual}}-F_{\mathrm{b}}$$

For example, if an object weighs 30 N and experiences an upward buoyant force of 10 N, its apparent weight as indicated by the supporting balance is 20 N.

The object's actual gravitational weight has not decreased. The smaller reading occurs because the surrounding fluid supplies part of the upward supporting force.

Applications of Archimedes' Principle

Floating Boats and Ships

A boat floats when it displaces enough water for the upward buoyant force to balance its total weight. Its hollow shape allows it to displace a substantial volume of water.

The same principle explains the flotation of fishing boats and cargo vessels along Gujarat's coastline and elsewhere.

Hydrometers

A hydrometer is an instrument used to determine the density or relative density of a liquid. Its floating position depends on the buoyant force supplied by the liquid.

Lactometers

A lactometer is a type of hydrometer used to assess the density of milk. The measured density can help indicate possible dilution, although density alone cannot establish every aspect of milk purity.

Submarines

A submarine changes its overall buoyancy by changing the amount of water in its ballast tanks. This enables it to sink, rise or remain submerged by changing the balance between its weight and buoyant force.

Prelims focus

  • Buoyant force acts vertically upward.
  • Archimedes' principle relates buoyant force to the weight of displaced fluid.
  • Buoyancy occurs in both liquids and gases.
  • A hydrometer measures liquid density or relative density.
  • A lactometer is used to assess milk density.
  • Trap: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid, not necessarily the weight of the immersed object.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 10, Gravitation, sections 10.5.2-10.6, printed pp. 140-142; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, Gravitation, sections 9.5.2-9.6, printed pp. 108-110.]

title: Buoyancy and Archimedes' Principle: Why Fluids Push Objects Upward

body:
Why Some Objects Float While Others Sink

A small iron nail generally sinks in water, whereas a much larger piece of cork may float. The difference cannot be explained by mass alone.

The important comparison is between the average density of the object and the density of the surrounding fluid, together with the buoyant force available to support the object.

Meaning of Density

Density is the mass contained in a unit volume of a substance or object.

Density is represented by the Greek letter \(\rho\) and is calculated as:

$$\rho=\frac{m}{V}$$

Here, \(m\) is mass and \(V\) is volume.

The SI unit of density is kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m3). Another commonly used unit is gram per cubic centimetre (g/cm3).

These units are related by:

$$1\;\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$$

The density of pure water is approximately 1000 kg/m3, or 1 g/cm3, near 4°C under ordinary pressure. This approximate value is commonly used in school-level calculations.

Density describes how much mass is present in a given volume. It does not mean that every dense object must have a large total mass. A small piece of iron may have less mass than a large piece of wood while still being much denser.

Density Depends on Material and Conditions

Different substances can have different densities because the same volume can contain different amounts of mass.

For a given substance, density can also change with temperature or pressure when its volume changes. Therefore, tabulated density values generally refer to specified physical conditions.

The distinction between material density and average density of an object is important. A hollow object may contain both solid material and enclosed air. Its overall average density depends on its total mass and total enclosed volume.

Relative Density

Comparing the density of a substance with that of water is often convenient.

Relative density is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water used as the reference.

$$\text{Relative density}=\frac{\text{Density of substance}}{\text{Density of water}}$$

Relative density is also called specific gravity in many elementary contexts.

Because the numerator and denominator have identical units, the units cancel. Therefore, relative density has no unit.

Example: Relative Density of a Substance

Suppose a substance has a density of 800 kg/m3. Using water's approximate density of 1000 kg/m3:

$$\text{Relative density}=\frac{800}{1000}=0.8$$

The substance has a relative density of 0.8. This means its density is 0.8 times the reference density of water.

Obtaining Density From Relative Density

If a substance has a relative density of 2.5 and the reference water density is 1000 kg/m3, its density is:

$$\rho=2.5\times1000=2500\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$$

Conditions for Floating, Remaining Suspended and Sinking

An object immersed in a liquid experiences 2 main forces relevant to floating: its weight acts downward, while buoyant force acts upward.

The resulting behaviour depends on the balance between these forces. For an ordinary rigid object, ignoring surface-tension effects and other external forces, comparing its overall average density with the liquid's density gives a useful prediction.

Average object densityBehaviourForce relationship
Less than liquid densityRises and floats partially immersedAt floating equilibrium, buoyancy equals weight
Equal to liquid densityCan remain fully immersed and suspendedBuoyancy equals weight
Greater than liquid densitySinks unless supported by another forceWhen fully immersed, weight exceeds buoyancy

Why a Floating Object Is Only Partially Immersed

Consider a block whose average density is less than that of water. When fully submerged, it can displace water weighing more than the block itself. The resulting buoyant force is greater than its weight, so the block rises.

As the block rises above the surface, its immersed volume decreases. It consequently displaces less water, reducing buoyant force.

It eventually reaches a floating position in which the buoyant force exactly balances its weight.

For an object floating freely in equilibrium, weight of the object = weight of the displaced fluid = buoyant force.

For example, a uniform block with relative density 0.8 floats in water with approximately 80% of its total volume immersed, assuming the reference densities apply and no other significant forces act on it.

Why an Iron Ship Can Float but an Iron Nail Sinks

An iron nail is compact and has a density much greater than that of water. Even when fully immersed, it cannot displace enough water for the resulting buoyant force to balance its weight. It therefore sinks.

A ship made partly of steel has a large hollow hull containing air. Its overall average density, considering the enclosed volume, can be lower than the density of water.

When placed in water, the ship displaces enough water to generate a buoyant force equal to its total weight. It then floats.

Thus, a ship does not float because steel itself is less dense than water. It floats because the ship's structure allows a sufficiently large volume of water to be displaced.

Why Objects Float More Easily in Salt Water

Dissolved salts generally increase the density of water. Therefore, seawater is usually denser than freshwater.

For the same immersed volume, denser seawater provides greater buoyant force than freshwater under comparable conditions.

A floating boat of unchanged weight therefore needs to displace a smaller volume of seawater to balance its weight. As a result, it generally floats slightly higher in seawater than in freshwater.

Worked Example: Predicting Whether an Object Will Sink

A solid object has a mass of 50 g and a volume of 20 cm3. Its density is:

$$\rho=\frac{50}{20}=2.5\;\mathrm{g/cm^3}$$

The density of water is approximately 1 g/cm3. Therefore, the object's relative density is:

$$\text{Relative density}=\frac{2.5}{1}=2.5$$

Because its density exceeds that of water, the object will sink when placed in water, provided no other supporting force is significant.

Connecting Gravitation, Pressure, Density and Buoyancy

These concepts are closely related. Gravitational attraction gives objects weight and helps produce pressure in fluids. Pressure differences within a fluid create an upward buoyant force. Archimedes' principle determines that force from the weight of displaced fluid. Comparing the object's weight with the available buoyant force explains floating and sinking.

Prelims focus

  • Density equals mass divided by volume.
  • The SI unit of density is kg/m3.
  • Water has an approximate density of 1000 kg/m3, or 1 g/cm3, near 4°C.
  • Relative density is a ratio and has no unit.
  • A freely floating object displaces fluid whose weight equals the object's weight.
  • Trap: Floating depends on overall average density and buoyancy, not simply on whether the object is heavy or made of metal.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 10, Gravitation, sections 10.5.3-10.7, printed pp. 140-145; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, Gravitation, sections 9.5.3-9.6 and associated chapter material, printed pp. 108-112; NCERT, Science, Class 6, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 4, Sorting Materials into Groups, section Objects May Float or Sink in Water, printed pp. 30-31.]
